rci9_site_effect_handling.detail: The paper explicitly mentions using Hierarchical Bayesian Regression to handle multi-site data. Hierarchical Bayesian regression (HBR) was used to develop a normative model as a function of age and sex for each brain region. HBR allows for the imposition of a common prior distribution across multiple sites to estimate site-specific means and variances.
rci9_site_effect_handling.supporting_text: To minimize the impact of site-related variability on subsequent results, hierarchical Bayesian regression (HBR) was employed in the HC cohort to develop a normative model of network degree centrality as a function of age and sex for each brain region (Fig. 1B). HBR allows for the imposition of a common prior distribution across multiple sites to estimate site-specific yet interrelated means and variances, thus accommodating signal and noise variability in multisite data while preserving meaningful site-related variations

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: k-means clustering to identify subtypes based on deviation maps. One-sample t-tests on deviation values for each subtype. Pearson correlation analyses between deviation values and HAMD scores. Two-sample t-tests to compare brain network deviations between subtypes. Partial least squares (PLS) regression analysis to explore the spatial correlation between cognitive functions and the observed deviations.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: The study identified two distinct MDD subtypes with opposing patterns of brain network degree centrality deviations between unimodal and transmodal networks, which were associated with different clinical and cognitive profiles.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: Using normative modeling on rs-fMRI data from 797 MDD patients and 822 controls, the study identified two MDD subtypes via k-means clustering of degree centrality deviation maps. Subtype 1 (55% of patients) showed positive deviations in LIM, FPN, and DMN, and negative deviations in VIS and SMN, correlating with higher cognitive functions. Subtype 2 (45%) showed the opposite pattern, with negative deviations in LIM, FPN, DMN and positive deviations in VIS and SMN, correlating with basic perceptual processes and more severe somatic symptoms. These findings reveal distinct neurobiological subtypes within MDD, offering a new framework for personalized medicine.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: 1. Cross-sectional design limits causal inference and observation of long-term associations. 2. Findings not yet validated with external data from different populations. 3. Incomplete clinical information (first-episode status, medication) for some patients. 4. Cognitive function analysis was at the group level, not individual.
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: Firstly, while normative models have provided valuable insights... the reliance on cross-sectional data has limited our capacity to observe longterm associations and establish causal relationships... Secondly, although the sample size of this study was commendable, our findings have not yet been validated with external data from different populations... Thirdly, the incomplete clinical information for certain MDD patients, such as their first-episode status and medication usage, constrained our thorough assessment... Lastly, this study has significantly advanced our understanding by analyzing cognitive functions at the group level.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: Subtypes were identified using k-means clustering on individual deviation maps. Neurosynth was used to analyze cognitive correlates of the identified subtypes. The study performed robustness checks using a different brain atlas (AAL90).

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: The study performed a validation analysis using the AAL90 atlas to confirm the robustness of the findings. The clustering results showed high stability across the two different atlases (Harvard-Oxford and AAL90), with an overall overlap rate of 0.726.
